K279.about: The ‘No. 1’ of Mozart’s eighteen sonatas is not really his first: he had already written several boyhood keyboard sonatas that never survived in print. This one opens the set of six he probably composed in Munich in early 1775, and its unusually rich dynamic and articulation markings — more detailed than in anything he had written before — led Mozart and his family to nickname the whole set the ‘difficult sonatas’ in later letters, apparently referring less to raw technical demands than to how much interpretive care they need. The opening Allegro is bright and confident; a gentle Andante follows; and the closing Allegro, built on quick, light figuration, sends the sonata off with real sparkle.
K279.ctx: Composed at the start of 1775 alongside its five companions K. 280–284, the sonata predates Mozart’s famous mature keyboard style but already shows an assured handling of classical form for a teenager not yet twenty. Only the manuscript of this sonata’s first movement is lost among the whole set of six; the rest survive in Mozart’s own hand. The six sonatas remained his only substantial set of original solo keyboard sonatas until he added three more in 1777–78.
facts: Composed in Munich in early 1775, the first of six sonatas Mozart’s family called the ‘difficult sonatas’.
Only this sonata’s first-movement manuscript is lost among the set of six.
Henle rates it level 6.

K280.about: The second of the six early sonatas has a special place among them for its middle movement, an Adagio in F minor built as a slow, aching siciliana — a rare moment of real melancholy this early in Mozart’s output. The outer movements are lighter: a graceful opening Allegro assai, and a finale, Presto, that dances along in triple time. The contrast between the wistful middle movement and its brighter neighbours gives the whole sonata a shape unusually satisfying for a work Mozart wrote in his teens.
K280.ctx: Composed alongside K. 279 and the rest of the set in early 1775, the sonata belongs to the group Mozart’s family called the ‘difficult sonatas’ for their unusually rich dynamic and articulation markings. The F-minor Adagio is often singled out by scholars and teachers alike as an early sign of the emotional depth Mozart would bring to slow movements throughout his career, well before the darker, more famous minor-key sonatas of his twenties.
parts: A slow, aching siciliana — an early moment of real melancholy.
A light, dancing finale in triple time.
facts: Its F-minor Adagio is often cited as an early sign of Mozart’s later emotional depth.
One of the six ‘difficult sonatas’ composed in Munich in early 1775.
Henle rates it level 5.

K281.about: A witty, well-proportioned sonata whose middle movement carries the unusual marking ‘Andante amoroso’ — tender and lyrical music, rare among Mozart’s tempo markings for its directness about mood. The outer movements are lighter and more conventional: a poised opening Allegro, and a closing rondo that dances along genially before a graceful final flourish.
K281.ctx: One of the six sonatas Mozart’s family later called the ‘difficult sonatas,’ composed in Munich in early 1775. For a long time this sonata was available only inside the larger complete Mozart volumes before Henle issued it as a stand-alone edition; its unusual ‘amoroso’ marking has made the middle movement a particular favourite among teachers introducing students to Mozart’s expressive range.
parts: A tender, lyrical slow movement with an unusually direct tempo marking.
facts: Its middle movement carries the rare marking ‘Andante amoroso’.
One of the six ‘difficult sonatas’ composed in Munich in early 1775.
Henle rates it level 5.

K282.about: An unconventional sonata among the six early ones for its order of movements: rather than opening fast, it begins with a slow, songful Adagio, followed by two minuets and only then a brisk closing Allegro. The effect is unusually reflective for a Mozart sonata opening, and the two minuets that follow are gentle rather than showy, making the sonata feel closer in spirit to a suite than to the more typical fast-slow-fast plan of its companions.
K282.ctx: Composed in Munich in early 1775 alongside its five companions, the sonata’s slow opening and paired minuets set it apart within the set of six ‘difficult sonatas’ Mozart’s family described in later correspondence. Its unusual structure has made it a favourite subject for discussions of how flexible Mozart’s early sense of sonata form already was, even before he settled into the more standardized patterns of his mature works.
parts: A slow, songful opening, unusual for beginning a sonata.
A pair of gentle minuets in place of a conventional middle movement.
facts: Opens with a slow movement rather than a fast one, unusual among Mozart’s sonatas.
Has two minuets rather than a single middle movement.
Henle rates it level 5.

K283.about: Curiously, this is the only one of Mozart’s eighteen piano sonatas — and one of only a handful among his piano concertos too — written in the pianistically grateful key of G major. It is one of the best-loved of the six early sonatas among teachers and students, not technically demanding but reliably effective in performance, especially in its extended closing Presto, marked with an exclamation-point-worthy urgency rare for a finale of this period.
K283.ctx: Composed in Munich at the start of 1775, the sonata belongs to the set of six Mozart’s family later called the ‘difficult sonatas.’ Its comparative technical ease relative to some of its companions, combined with its consistently rewarding, well-balanced writing, has made it one of the most frequently taught of all eighteen sonatas, a reliable favourite decades before Mozart wrote the even more famous ‘easy’ sonata K. 545.
facts: The only one of Mozart’s eighteen piano sonatas in G major.
One of the most frequently taught of the eighteen sonatas.
Henle rates it level 5.

K284.about: The last and most ambitious of the six early sonatas, which Mozart carried with him as a calling-card when he set off for Paris in 1777, having already performed it successfully in Munich, Augsburg and Mannheim. It is unusually rich in dynamic markings and formal invention for its date, including a middle movement titled Rondeau en Polonaise — a slow, stately dance rather than a conventional Andante — and a finale that is itself a substantial theme with twelve variations, giving the whole sonata a scale closer to a concerto than to its five companions.
K284.ctx: Composed in 1775 to close the set of six ‘difficult sonatas,’ K. 284 was clearly a showpiece Mozart was proud of: he told his father how well it had gone over on his travels. It was eventually published on its own in 1784, separately from its five companions, reflecting its status as the most substantial and virtuosic of the group. Its scale anticipates the more expansive individual sonatas Mozart would write later in Paris and Vienna.
parts: A confident, richly detailed opening movement.
A stately, dance-like slow movement in place of a conventional Andante.
A substantial theme and twelve variations serving as the finale.
facts: Mozart carried it as a showpiece on his 1777 journey to Paris.
Its finale is a theme and twelve variations rather than a conventional fast movement.
Henle rates it level 6.

K309.about: A brilliant showpiece written during Mozart’s stay in Mannheim, home to one of Europe’s finest orchestras and a hotbed of the new, dramatic ‘Mannheim style’ — sudden crescendos, sweeping scales, orchestral effects transplanted to the keyboard. Mozart himself said the Andante was intended as a musical portrait of Rosa Cannabich, the teenage daughter of the Mannheim orchestra’s director, capturing what he called her own poised, deliberate character in music.
K309.ctx: Composed in 1777 while Mozart was traveling with his mother in search of a permanent post, the sonata reflects the glamour and virtuosity of the Mannheim court he was courting for a job. He described in a letter how he shaped the Andante specifically to suit Rosa Cannabich’s temperament as he understood it, an unusually personal anecdote about a purely instrumental slow movement. The sonata was later published together with K. 310 and K. 311 as a group.
parts: A brilliant, orchestrally-conceived opening movement in the Mannheim style.
A poised slow movement said to portray Rosa Cannabich.
facts: Mozart said the Andante was a musical portrait of Rosa Cannabich, daughter of the Mannheim orchestra's director.
Written in the ‘Mannheim style’, known for its dramatic orchestral effects.
Henle rates it level 6.

K310.about: A dark, tragic sonata and one of only two of Mozart’s eighteen piano sonatas in a minor key. Composed in Paris in 1778, it is often linked to the death of his mother that same summer, though no direct evidence ties the two together, and Mozart scholars generally caution against reading the sonata as a literal musical diary entry. Whatever its origin, the music itself is unusually stormy and unsettled for its date, with a driving, agitated first movement, a searching Andante, and a restless, syncopated finale.
K310.ctx: Mozart’s mother, Anna Maria, died in Paris on 3 July 1778 while accompanying him on the journey that produced this sonata, among other works. The sole authoritative source for the Urtext text is Mozart’s own autograph manuscript, since the first printed edition of 1781, issued alongside K. 309 and K. 311, is riddled with errors. The sonata remains one of the most performed and recorded of the eighteen, prized for its emotional directness.
facts: One of only two of Mozart’s eighteen piano sonatas in a minor key.
Composed in Paris in 1778, the same summer his mother died there.
Henle rates it level 6.

K311.about: A bright, energetic sonata from the same Mannheim journey that produced K. 309, sharing some of that sonata’s brilliant, orchestrally-inspired keyboard writing but with a sunnier disposition overall. The finale is a spirited rondo whose returning theme grows more elaborate with each appearance, giving the movement real momentum and charm.
K311.ctx: Composed in 1777 during Mozart’s extended stay in Mannheim while he searched for a permanent musical appointment, the sonata was later published together with K. 309 and K. 310 as a set, though the three were written under different circumstances and with different characters. It remains a favourite among the ‘Mannheim’ sonatas for its consistently good-humoured, outgoing tone.
parts: A spirited rondo whose theme grows more elaborate with each return.
facts: Composed during the same 1777 Mannheim journey that produced K. 309.
Later published together with K. 309 and K. 310 as a set.
Henle rates it level 6.

K330.about: A graceful, lyrical sonata and one of a set of three, K. 330–332, that mark Mozart’s return to the genre after several years focused on concertos and chamber music. Its slow movement, an Andante cantabile, is especially tender, and its outer movements combine the poise of his earlier style with the fuller keyboard textures he had developed writing piano concertos in the intervening years.
K330.ctx: The exact date and place of composition of K. 330–332 has long been debated by scholars, with older accounts placing them in Paris in 1778 and more recent research favouring Vienna or Salzburg around 1783; Henle’s Urtext edition follows the later dating. Whichever is correct, the three sonatas show a more assured, concerto-influenced pianism than Mozart’s earlier sets, reflecting the years he had spent since 1775 writing for a public increasingly familiar with his mature keyboard style.
facts: Part of a set of three sonatas, K. 330–332, whose date of composition scholars have long debated.
Henle’s Urtext edition favours a Vienna or Salzburg dating around 1783.
Henle rates it level 5.

K331.about: Probably the most famous of all Mozart’s piano sonatas, thanks entirely to its finale, the ‘Rondo alla turca’ — a sparkling imitation of Ottoman Janissary band music, complete with the percussive, drum-like effects that were a craze in Vienna at the time. Unusually, the sonata has no sonata-form movement at all: it opens instead with a theme and six variations, followed by a minuet, before the famous Turkish rondo closes the work in a blaze of glittering octaves.
K331.ctx: Composed around 1783, alongside K. 330 and K. 332, the sonata’s ‘Turkish’ finale reflects a broader Viennese fashion for exoticized Ottoman musical style, heard also in works by Haydn and later Beethoven. The finale has taken on a life entirely of its own, arranged and excerpted far more often than the sonata as a whole; the opening variation movement and minuet, though less famous, are considered by pianists to be subtler and more rewarding music. Henle’s edition of this sonata was substantially updated in 2015 based on renewed source study.
parts: A gentle theme followed by six variations, in place of an opening sonata-form movement.
The famous finale imitating Ottoman Janissary band music.
facts: Its ‘Rondo alla turca’ finale is probably the most famous single movement in all of Mozart’s piano music.
The sonata has no conventional sonata-form movement at all.
Henle rates it level 6.

K332.about: The most richly contrasted of the three sonatas K. 330–332, its first movement moving through an unusually wide range of moods and keys for a work of its date, including a stormy minor-key episode that briefly darkens the otherwise sunny opening. The finale is brilliant and virtuosic, full of rapid scales and wide leaps that make it one of the more technically demanding movements among Mozart’s early and middle-period sonatas.
K332.ctx: Composed around 1783 alongside its two companions, the sonata shows Mozart experimenting with greater dramatic contrast within a single movement than in his earlier, more evenly-tempered sonatas — a trait that would become more pronounced in his later solo keyboard works. Its combination of lyrical writing and genuine virtuosity has made it a popular recital choice among the three sonatas of the set.
parts: A richly contrasted movement including a stormy minor-key episode.
A brilliant, technically demanding finale of scales and leaps.
facts: Part of the set of three sonatas, K. 330–332, composed around 1783.
Its finale is one of the more technically demanding among Mozart’s middle-period sonatas.
Henle rates it level 6.

K333.about: A lyrical, concerto-like sonata that stands apart from the K. 330–332 set it followed, its finale built almost like a small piano concerto movement, complete with a written-out cadenza near the end — a feature almost unheard of in a solo sonata at the time. The influence of Johann Christian Bach, whose keyboard style Mozart had long admired, is audible throughout, particularly in the flowing, songful main themes.
K333.ctx: Composed in late 1783, probably while Mozart was passing through Linz on the journey home from Salzburg that also produced the ‘Linz’ Symphony, the sonata is sometimes classified with the earlier K. 330–332 set but is generally understood by scholars as a separate, slightly later work with its own distinct character. Its concerto-like finale, with a full written cadenza, anticipates the grander scale of some of Mozart’s later keyboard writing.
parts: A lyrical, flowing opening movement showing the influence of J. C. Bach.
A songful, richly ornamented slow movement.
A concerto-like finale with a written-out cadenza near the end.
facts: Its finale includes a written-out cadenza, almost unheard of in a solo sonata of the period.
Probably composed in Linz in late 1783, around the same time as the ‘Linz’ Symphony.
Henle rates it level 6.

K457.about: A stormy, dramatic sonata in C minor, often performed and published together with the Fantasy in the same key, K. 475, which Mozart wrote two years later as an expansive introduction to it. Together the two works form one of Mozart’s most powerful statements for solo keyboard, their shared key and turbulent character anticipating the C-minor world Beethoven would later make his own in works like the ‘Pathétique’ Sonata, which scholars believe Beethoven knew and was influenced by.
K457.ctx: Composed in 1784 and published in 1785 on its own, the sonata was joined two years later by the Fantasy K. 475, and the two have been published and performed together ever since as a single dramatic sequence. Mozart dedicated the pairing to his pupil Therese von Trattner; the C-minor intensity of both works stood apart from the generally lighter character of Mozart’s Viennese instrumental music of the mid-1780s, and it left a clear mark on the next generation of composers.
parts: A serene, songful slow movement in contrast to the outer movements.
facts: Usually performed and published together with the Fantasy in C minor, K. 475.
Its C-minor intensity is thought to have influenced Beethoven’s own C-minor works.
Henle rates it level 7.

K533.about: A contrapuntal, intellectually rigorous sonata assembled by Mozart from two different periods of composition: he wrote the first two movements in 1788, then reached back to a Rondo, K. 494, he had composed two years earlier and reworked it into a substantial new finale to complete the sonata. The result is denser and more contrapuntally worked than most of Mozart’s earlier sonatas, reflecting his renewed study of Bach and Handel’s fugal writing in the years after 1782.
K533.ctx: Composed in stages between 1786 and 1788, the sonata is one of the clearest instrumental examples of what Mozart called incorporating the ‘learned style’ of counterpoint into his otherwise ‘galant’ musical language, a synthesis he pursued increasingly in his last Vienna years across works from the ‘Jupiter’ Symphony to the Requiem. The reworked Rondo finale, K. 494/533, shows Mozart returning to and substantially revising his own earlier material, a relatively unusual practice for him.
parts: A searching, harmonically adventurous slow movement.
A substantial finale reworked from an independent Rondo, K. 494, composed two years earlier.
facts: Its finale began as an independent Rondo, K. 494, written two years before the rest of the sonata.
Reflects Mozart’s renewed study of Bach and Handel’s counterpoint in his last Vienna years.
Henle rates it level 6.

K545.about: Mozart entered this sonata into his own thematic catalogue as ‘a little piano sonata for beginners,’ and it has been known ever since as the ‘Sonata facile’ or ‘Sonata semplice’ — though pianists who study it closely tend to agree that its transparent textures leave absolutely nowhere for a player to hide. The famous opening Allegro is built almost entirely from simple scales and Alberti-bass patterns, deceptively easy to read and genuinely difficult to play with the poise Mozart’s spare writing demands.
K545.ctx: Composed in 1788, the same year as his three last symphonies, the sonata’s nickname does not come from Mozart himself but from the title page of its first edition, printed only after his death. It remains one of the most widely taught pieces in the entire piano repertoire, usually a student’s first encounter with Mozart, even as generations of teachers have pointed out that its apparent simplicity is one of its greatest challenges.
parts: A deceptively simple opening built from scales and Alberti-bass figures.
A graceful slow movement with a brief minor-key turn.
facts: Mozart himself described it in his catalogue as ‘a little piano sonata for beginners’.
Its ‘Sonata facile’ nickname comes from its posthumous first edition, not from Mozart.
Henle rates it level 5.

K570.about: A late sonata of refined, transparent simplicity, written in the same productive burst as K. 576 but far gentler in character. Its textures are unusually spare even by Mozart’s standards, with long stretches of two-voice writing that demand real clarity and evenness from the performer despite the music’s outwardly modest difficulty.
K570.ctx: Composed in 1789, around the time Mozart was hoping to write a set of easy sonatas for Princess Friederike of Prussia — a plan that in the end produced only K. 576 — the sonata shares something of that intended simplicity without being directly part of the commission. It was not published until 1796, five years after Mozart’s death, and remains less frequently performed than many of his other late works despite its considerable charm.
facts: Composed in 1789, around the time of Mozart’s plan to write easy sonatas for Princess Friederike of Prussia.
Not published until 1796, five years after his death.
Henle rates it level 5.

K576.about: Mozart’s eighteenth and final piano sonata, and by common consent among pianists and Henle’s own editors, quite possibly the most technically demanding of the whole set — a striking outcome, since he originally planned it as the first of six easy sonatas for Princess Friederike of Prussia. Only this one was ever written, and its dense, contrapuntal writing, wide leaps and constant imitative interplay between the hands earned it the English nickname ‘Hunt Sonata,’ after the horn-call-like arpeggios that open the first movement.
K576.ctx: Composed in the summer of 1789 as part of a commission for the Prussian princess that never progressed beyond this single sonata, K. 576 shows Mozart at his most contrapuntally ambitious in a solo keyboard work, closer in spirit to the fugal writing of the ‘Jupiter’ Symphony finale than to anything in his earlier sonatas. It was published in 1791, the year of Mozart’s death, and closes the cycle of eighteen sonatas on its most demanding note rather than its simplest.
parts: A contrapuntally dense opening movement, opening with a horn-call figure that gave the sonata its ‘Hunt’ nickname.
A songful, richly ornamented slow movement.
facts: Originally planned as the first of six easy sonatas for Princess Friederike of Prussia; only this one was written.
Nicknamed the ‘Hunt Sonata’ in English after its opening horn-call figure.
Henle rates it level 7, the highest of all eighteen sonatas.

K466.about: The first of only two Mozart piano concertos in a minor key, and one of the most dramatic works he ever wrote for the instrument — a clear ancestor of the stormy Romantic piano concertos that would follow decades later. The turbulent, syncopated opening movement gives way to a serene Romanze, twice interrupted by an agitated minor-key episode, and a fiery finale that only turns to D major, and to triumph, in its closing bars.
K466.ctx: Composed at extraordinary speed in early 1785 — the parts were reportedly still being copied on the morning of the premiere, which Mozart’s father Leopold witnessed on a visit to Vienna — the concerto marks a new level of dramatic intensity in Mozart’s concerto writing. Beethoven admired it enough to write his own cadenzas for the first and third movements, which remain the most frequently performed today, and the work’s stormy character made it a favourite of early Romantic composers who saw in it a forerunner of their own concerto style.
parts: A serene slow movement twice interrupted by an agitated minor-key episode.
A fiery finale that turns to triumph only in its closing bars.
facts: One of only two Mozart piano concertos in a minor key.
Beethoven wrote cadenzas for it, still the most commonly used today.
The orchestral parts were reportedly still being copied on the morning of the premiere.

K467.about: A brilliant, festive concerto that has become one of Mozart’s most famous works for an unlikely reason: its serene, unhurried second movement was used on the soundtrack of the 1967 Swedish film Elvira Madigan, which introduced it to a huge popular audience and gave the concerto its enduring nickname. The outer movements are grander and more martial, with trumpets and drums giving the work real ceremonial weight, in clear contrast to the hushed, almost weightless Andante at its centre.
K467.ctx: Composed in 1785, just a month after the D-minor Concerto K. 466, the C-major Concerto shows an entirely different side of Mozart’s concerto writing — bright and outward-facing rather than stormy. It was completed so close to its premiere that Mozart reportedly had not had time to write out the piano part in full and played some of it from memory or improvisation at the first performance. Its ‘Elvira Madigan’ nickname postdates Mozart by nearly two centuries but has stuck ever since the film's release.
parts: A grand, ceremonial opening movement with trumpets and drums.
The famous serene slow movement later used in the film Elvira Madigan.
facts: Its slow movement gave the concerto its nickname after being used in the 1967 film Elvira Madigan.
Completed so close to its premiere that Mozart may have improvised parts of the piano writing.
Composed only a month after the D-minor Concerto, K. 466.

K622.about: Mozart’s last completed instrumental work and one of the great farewells in music, written for his friend the clarinettist Anton Stadler just weeks before Mozart’s death. Originally conceived for Stadler’s custom-built ‘basset clarinet,’ with an extended lower range not found on the standard instrument, the concerto is serene and autumnal in character, its famous slow movement in particular radiating a calm that has made it a favourite for films, weddings and memorial services alike.
K622.ctx: Composed in September and October 1791, in the same extraordinary final months that also produced The Magic Flute and the unfinished Requiem, the concerto was written for Anton Stadler, a virtuoso clarinettist and close friend of Mozart’s who had commissioned instrument makers to extend the clarinet’s range downward specifically for this kind of writing. Because basset clarinets fell out of use after Stadler’s time, the concerto is most often performed today on a standard A clarinet, with some of the lowest notes transposed up an octave — a compromise modern scholarship and specially built reproduction basset clarinets have increasingly tried to correct.
parts: A famous, serenely lyrical slow movement.
facts: Mozart’s last completed instrumental work, finished weeks before his death.
Written for the clarinettist Anton Stadler and his extended-range ‘basset clarinet.’
Composed in the same final months as The Magic Flute and the unfinished Requiem.

K581.about: A warm, autumnal work written for the same friend, Anton Stadler, who would later inspire the Clarinet Concerto, and one of the first great works ever written for the combination of clarinet and string quartet. The clarinet is treated as a genuine equal partner rather than a soloist accompanied by strings, weaving in and out of the quartet's texture, and the whole work has a relaxed, songful warmth that has made it one of the most beloved pieces of chamber music in the repertoire.
K581.ctx: Composed in 1789, two years before the Clarinet Concerto, the quintet was written for Anton Stadler and first performed at a concert of the Viennese musicians' society in December of that year, with Stadler himself playing the clarinet part. Like the concerto that followed it, the quintet was originally conceived with Stadler's extended-range basset clarinet in mind, and modern players sometimes use a basset clarinet or a specially adapted instrument to restore the very lowest notes Mozart wrote for him.
parts: A songful slow movement showcasing the clarinet's tone.
A minuet with two contrasting trios.
facts: Written for the clarinettist Anton Stadler, who also inspired the Clarinet Concerto two years later.
One of the first major works for clarinet and string quartet.
Originally conceived for Stadler's extended-range basset clarinet.

K525.about: Almost certainly the most famous piece of classical music ever written, ‘A Little Night Music’ is a compact, sunny serenade for string orchestra that Mozart entered into his own catalogue of works with no further explanation of its purpose — no commission, no dedicatee, no occasion is recorded. Its opening bars are recognisable to millions of people who have never otherwise heard a note of Mozart, and its four short, elegant movements have made it a fixture of concert programmes, films and adverts ever since.
K525.ctx: Mozart entered the piece into his own thematic catalogue on 10 August 1787, during the same summer he was completing Don Giovanni, though nothing else is known about why he wrote it. The autograph score originally included a second minuet, now lost, meaning the familiar four-movement version heard today may not be quite what Mozart first intended. It was not published until 1827, decades after his death, and its universal popularity today stands in odd contrast to how little Mozart himself apparently thought to say about it.
facts: Possibly the most widely recognised piece of classical music ever written.
Mozart recorded no reason for composing it in his own catalogue of works.
The autograph score shows it originally had a second minuet, now lost.

K550.about: One of only two symphonies Mozart wrote in a minor key, and among the most urgent, restless works in his entire output — its opening bars, a quietly agitated string figure under a plaintive melody, are instantly recognisable even to listeners who know nothing else about the piece. The symphony maintains an unusually consistent mood of anxious intensity across all four movements, including the minuet, which is tense and driven rather than graceful, a striking choice for a dance movement.
K550.ctx: Composed in the summer of 1788 as the second of Mozart’s last three symphonies, written in an extraordinary burst of roughly six weeks alongside the ‘Jupiter’ and No. 39, K. 550 was almost certainly never performed during Mozart’s lifetime — no evidence survives of a contemporary performance, and it is unclear why he wrote it at all, since he had no commission or occasion on record. It was later revised to add clarinets to the orchestration, and this version, alongside the original without clarinets, are both still performed today.
parts: A restless, urgent opening movement built from a quietly agitated string figure.
A calmer but still unsettled slow movement.
A tense, driven minuet, unusually serious for a dance movement.
K550.sc: 1 flute, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets (added in revision), 2 bassoons, 2 horns, strings
facts: One of only two Mozart symphonies in a minor key.
Composed in a six-week burst alongside his last two symphonies.
No evidence survives that it was ever performed in Mozart’s lifetime.

K551.about: Mozart’s last symphony and his grandest, nicknamed ‘Jupiter’ by an English impresario decades after Mozart’s death, not by Mozart himself. Its finale is the work’s crowning achievement: a dazzling fusion of sonata form and fugue, weaving together five independent melodic ideas in ever more complex counterpoint until all five sound together at once in the closing bars — a feat of contrapuntal engineering rarely equalled in the symphonic literature.
K551.ctx: Completed in August 1788 as the last of the three symphonies Mozart wrote in a single extraordinary summer, alongside No. 39 and the G-minor Symphony K. 550, the ‘Jupiter’ was almost certainly never performed in his lifetime, like its companions. The nickname is generally credited to the impresario Johann Peter Salomon, who brought Haydn to London and who may have coined it to suggest the symphony's godlike grandeur; it has stuck ever since, even though Mozart never knew it by that name.
parts: A dazzling finale combining sonata form with five-voice fugue.
K551.sc: 2 flutes, 2 oboes, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, 2 trumpets, timpani, strings
facts: Its ‘Jupiter’ nickname was coined after Mozart's death, likely by the impresario Johann Peter Salomon.
The finale combines sonata form with a five-voice fugue, a rare feat in symphonic writing.
The last of three symphonies Mozart wrote in a single summer in 1788.

K620.prem: 30 September 1791, Theater auf der Wieden, Vienna
K620.about: A fairy-tale Singspiel mixing spoken dialogue with music, written for a popular suburban Viennese theatre rather than the court opera house, and one of the last works Mozart completed before his death barely two months after its premiere. Beneath its story of trials, magic and enlightenment — the prince Tamino and the bird-catcher Papageno searching for love while the priest Sarastro and the vengeful Queen of the Night contest for power — lie layers of Masonic symbolism, reflecting Mozart's own membership in a Viennese Masonic lodge.
K620.ctx: Composed in 1791 for Emanuel Schikaneder, an actor-manager, fellow Freemason and the opera's librettist, who also created the role of Papageno at the premiere. Mozart conducted the first performances himself and continued attending them throughout the final weeks of his life; a letter he wrote to his wife just weeks before he died describes listening to a performance from backstage and mentally following along with delight. It remains one of the most frequently staged operas in the world.
parts: A masonically-tinged overture with three solemn chords.
The Queen of the Night's first, dramatic aria.
The Queen of the Night's famous, fiendishly virtuosic second aria.
Sarastro's noble aria of wisdom and forgiveness.
A triumphant conclusion celebrating love and enlightenment.
facts: Written for a popular suburban theatre, not the Viennese court opera.
Its librettist, Emanuel Schikaneder, also created the role of Papageno.
Mozart died less than ten weeks after conducting its premiere.

K527.about: A dark comedy about seduction, defiance and supernatural punishment, telling the story of the unrepentant seducer Don Giovanni, who is finally dragged down to hell by the animated statue of a man he murdered. Mozart and his librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte labelled it a ‘dramma giocoso,’ a mixed genre that lets the opera swing between broad comedy, genuine menace and, in its famous final scene, real supernatural terror, all within the same evening.
K527.ctx: Composed for Prague, a city that had embraced Mozart's Marriage of Figaro more warmly than Vienna had, the opera was written to a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte, who also wrote Figaro and Così fan tutte, completing Mozart's celebrated trilogy of Da Ponte operas. According to a much-repeated but unverifiable story, Mozart wrote the overture the night before the premiere, finishing it only hours before the performance. The opera was an immediate triumph in Prague, though it was received more coolly at its later Vienna premiere.
parts: An overture reportedly written the night before the premiere.
A seductive duet between Don Giovanni and Zerlina.
Leporello's comic ‘catalogue aria’ listing his master's conquests.
Don Ottavio's tender aria of devotion.
The statue of the Commendatore drags Don Giovanni down to hell.
facts: The second of three operas Mozart wrote with the librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte.
Legend holds Mozart wrote the overture the night before the premiere.
Its subtitle, ‘dramma giocoso,’ signals its mix of comedy and genuine menace.

K492.about: A comedy of love, class and forgiveness set over one frantic day, in which the servant Figaro and his fiancée Susanna outwit their philandering aristocratic employer, Count Almaviva, who is scheming to claim Susanna for himself. Based on a French play that had been banned in Vienna for its perceived attack on aristocratic privilege, the opera softens some of its source's political edge while keeping its sympathy firmly with the servants rather than their masters — a genuinely daring stance for a court composer to take.
K492.ctx: Composed in 1785–86 to a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte, adapted from Beaumarchais's play The Marriage of Figaro, the opera required special permission from Emperor Joseph II to be staged at all, since the original play was banned in the Habsburg lands. Mozart and Da Ponte's version passed the censors, and the opera premiered in Vienna in May 1786 to a warm reception, though it found its most enthusiastic audience in Prague later that year — success that directly led to the commission for Don Giovanni.
parts: Figaro's defiant aria vowing to outwit the Count.
Cherubino's breathless aria about the confusions of adolescent love.
The Countess's poignant aria mourning her husband's lost affection.
A joyful reconciliation closing the opera.
facts: Based on a French play that had been banned in Vienna for attacking aristocratic privilege.
Required special imperial permission from Joseph II to be staged.
Its success in Prague led directly to the commission for Don Giovanni.

K618.about: A brief, serene motet for choir and strings, composed for the feast of Corpus Christi and among the last sacred works Mozart completed before his death that same year. Barely three minutes long, it is a model of concentrated simplicity: a single, unbroken flow of chordal harmony setting a medieval Latin text about the body of Christ, without a single ornamental flourish or virtuosic passage anywhere in the score.
K618.ctx: Composed in June 1791 for Anton Stoll, the choirmaster at Baden bei Wien, a spa town near Vienna where Mozart's wife Constanze was taking the waters during her pregnancy, the motet was written for a modest parish choir rather than a grand cathedral ensemble, which helps explain its plain, unadorned style. Despite, or perhaps because of, its simplicity, it has become one of Mozart's most beloved and frequently performed sacred works, sung in churches and concert halls alike.
facts: Composed for a small parish choir in the spa town of Baden bei Wien.
Written for the feast of Corpus Christi in June 1791, the year of Mozart's death.
Despite its brevity, it is one of Mozart's most frequently performed sacred works.

K626.about: Mozart's last work, left unfinished at his death and completed from his sketches by his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr. Commissioned anonymously by a nobleman who wished to pass the work off as his own composition, the Requiem has since become wrapped in legend, most persistently the myth, popularised by the play and film Amadeus, that it was commissioned by a mysterious figure connected to Mozart's death — a story with almost no basis in the historical record, but one that has permanently shaped how the piece is heard.
K626.ctx: Mozart worked on the Requiem through the autumn of 1791 while also completing The Magic Flute and the Clarinet Concerto, but died in December with the score only partly finished — he had completed the Introit fully and sketched substantial parts of the remaining movements, but the Lacrimosa breaks off after only eight bars. His widow Constanze, needing to deliver the commissioned work to be paid, had Süssmayr complete it from Mozart's sketches and his own knowledge of Mozart's intentions, and it is this completed version, imperfect and debated by scholars ever since, that is almost always performed today.
parts: The only movement Mozart completed entirely in his own hand.
A tense, fugal plea for mercy.
A terrifying vision of the day of judgment.
The famous, mournful movement Mozart left unfinished after eight bars.
A vivid depiction of the damned, contrasted with a prayer for mercy.
K626.sc: Soprano, alto, tenor and bass soloists, chorus, orchestra
facts: Left unfinished at Mozart's death and completed by his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr.
The famous myth of a mysterious commissioner tied to Mozart's death has little historical basis.
The Lacrimosa breaks off after only eight bars in Mozart's own hand.

K175.about: Mozart’s first entirely original piano concerto — not arranged from other composers’ sonata movements, as his very earliest concertos had been — written at seventeen. It is confident and full of orchestral colour for so young a composer, particularly its horn and oboe writing. Mozart kept it in his own performing repertoire for a decade, and in 1782 wrote a new rondo finale, K. 382, for Vienna audiences, judging the original finale old-fashioned by then.
K175.ctx: Composed in December 1773 after Mozart’s return from Vienna, the concerto shows him absorbing the galant concerto style then fashionable while already finding an individual voice in its wind writing. That he kept performing it into his Vienna years shows how highly he regarded it even after composing his mature masterpieces.
parts: A bright, confident opening movement for a composer barely seventeen.
A vigorous closing movement, later replaced in Vienna by the rondo K. 382.
facts: Mozart’s first entirely original piano concerto.
He wrote a new finale, the Rondo K. 382, for it in Vienna in 1782.
It remained part of his own concert repertoire for about a decade.

K238.about: A genial, compact concerto written for Mozart’s own use in Salzburg’s court and private concerts, marked by an unusually prominent, almost operatic slow movement and a playful finale in triple metre. Less often performed today than the concertos that follow it, it shows Mozart refining the balance between soloist and orchestra that would define his mature concertos.
K238.ctx: Composed in January 1776, in the midst of a run of concertos Mozart wrote for himself to play in Salzburg. Coming shortly after K. 175, it shows a marked growth in the interplay between piano and orchestra, particularly the woodwind writing.
parts: A lyrical, almost vocal slow movement.
A light, dancing finale in triple metre.
facts: Written for Mozart’s own concerts in Salzburg in 1776.
Its slow movement is notably song-like, almost operatic in character.
It was not published during Mozart’s lifetime.

K271.about: Widely regarded as Mozart’s first unquestioned masterpiece in the concerto form, written at twenty-one for a visiting virtuosa long known only by the nickname ‘Jeunehomme’ (identified by scholars in 2004 as Victoire Jenamy, daughter of the choreographer Jean-Georges Noverre). It breaks convention from its opening bars, where the soloist interrupts the orchestra’s very first phrase instead of waiting for a long introduction, and its slow movement is an unusually tragic C-minor lament, rare for a concerto of this period. The finale’s rondo is itself interrupted by a stately minuet before its final dash to the close.
K271.ctx: Composed in January 1777, shortly before Mozart’s long journey to Mannheim and Paris, the concerto shows a sudden leap in ambition and structural daring beyond anything in his five previous piano concertos.
parts: The soloist enters after only a single orchestral bar, breaking convention.
An unusually tragic, aria-like slow movement.
A brilliant finale interrupted by a stately minuet before its close.
facts: The soloist enters after just one bar of orchestral introduction, unusual for its time.
Its dedicatee, long known only as ‘Jeunehomme’, was identified as Victoire Jenamy in 2004.
The finale’s rondo pauses for a formal minuet before its close.

K414.about: The first of three concertos Mozart wrote in his first year in Vienna as he established himself as a freelance composer-performer. He advertised all three as playable either with full orchestra or, more modestly, with string quartet alone — a practical touch aimed at amateur purchasers who might lack an orchestra. Its slow movement quotes a theme from an overture by J. C. Bach, Mozart’s early mentor, who had recently died, apparently as a tribute.
K414.ctx: Composed in late 1782 as Mozart settled in Vienna after leaving Salzburg, the concerto was designed for maximum commercial appeal, attractive to professional and amateur performers alike, as Mozart sought subscribers for a concert series and for publication of the scores.
parts: A graceful opening movement in Mozart’s newly confident Vienna style.
A tender slow movement quoting a theme by J. C. Bach.
K414.sc: Solo piano and orchestra (or piano and string quartet)
facts: Can be performed with string quartet alone instead of full orchestra.
Its slow movement quotes a theme by J. C. Bach as a tribute after his death.
One of the first works Mozart composed as a freelance musician in Vienna.

K449.about: Written for Mozart’s talented pupil Barbara Ployer, this concerto opens a remarkable run of concertos composed in 1784 alone. Mozart entered it as the very first work in the thematic catalogue he began keeping that February, marking a new stage of professional organisation in his career. More intimately scored than the concertos that immediately follow, it can be played with a small string ensemble alone.
K449.ctx: Composed in February 1784 for his pupil Barbara Ployer, who performed it at a concert Mozart’s father Leopold attended and praised in a letter home. It marks the start of the thematic catalogue Mozart kept meticulously until his death.
parts: An energetic opening in a concise, chamber-like texture.
A spirited finale with a fugal episode.
K449.sc: Solo piano and orchestra (oboes and horns optional)
facts: The first entry in the thematic catalogue Mozart began keeping in 1784.
Written for his pupil Barbara Ployer.
Can be performed with a reduced string ensemble.

K450.about: One of a pair of concertos, with K. 451, that Mozart wrote in March 1784 for his own subscription concerts, and one he described in a letter to his father as demanding enough to make the performer ‘sweat’ — a mark of its virtuosic writing, especially for the wind instruments, which he called the piano’s ‘concertante’ partners. It shows his growing fondness for elaborate wind dialogue with the soloist.
K450.ctx: Composed in March 1784 during Mozart’s busiest concert season, when he wrote and performed several concertos in quick succession. He specifically praised the demanding, virtuosic wind writing in this concerto in a letter to his father.
parts: A brilliant movement with prominent, virtuosic wind writing.
A set of variations forming the slow movement.
facts: Mozart described its wind writing as demanding enough to make performers ‘sweat’.
Composed in the same month as its companion, K. 451.
Its slow movement is a set of variations.

K451.about: Written immediately after K. 450, this concerto shares its brilliant, festive character, with trumpets and drums lending martial colour absent from most of Mozart’s other Vienna concertos. Mozart considered it, alongside its companion, among the most demanding and satisfying of his concertos to date.
K451.ctx: Composed within days of K. 450 in March 1784, during an extraordinarily productive stretch of concerto writing. Mozart wrote to his father that this pair, along with K. 453, represented works ‘to make the performer sweat’, underlining their technical ambition.
parts: A festive opening with trumpets and drums.
facts: One of three concertos Mozart wrote within weeks of each other in spring 1784.
Uses trumpets and drums, unusual among his piano concertos.
Mozart singled it out, with K. 450, as especially demanding to perform.

K453.about: Composed for Barbara Ployer, who premiered it at a concert Mozart also attended with the visiting composer Giovanni Paisiello. The concerto is tied to a famous anecdote: shortly after finishing it, Mozart bought a pet starling that could sing a close variant of the finale’s main theme, and he later wrote a small lament in his household expense book when the bird died three years afterward.
K453.ctx: Composed in the spring of 1784 for Barbara Ployer’s concert, at which Mozart also performed the concerto K. 449. The starling story comes from an entry in Mozart’s own expense book, where he transcribed the bird’s version of the theme alongside his own.
parts: A graceful opening movement Mozart’s pet starling reportedly could whistle.
A wide-ranging, almost operatic slow movement.
A theme-and-variations finale ending in a comic, breathless Presto.
facts: Mozart’s pet starling could reportedly sing a version of the finale’s theme.
Written for and premiered by his pupil Barbara Ployer.
Its finale ends with an unusually comic, fast coda.

K456.about: Long associated with the blind Viennese virtuosa Maria Theresia von Paradis, though modern scholarship questions whether it was written for her specifically. Leopold Mozart, hearing his son perform it in Vienna, wrote home that it moved him to tears. Its G-minor slow movement, a set of variations, is one of Mozart’s most affecting.
K456.ctx: Composed in September 1784, it was among the concertos Leopold Mozart heard during his visit to Vienna in early 1785, an occasion he described movingly in letters to his daughter, praising both the music and his son’s playing.
parts: A poignant set of variations forming the slow movement.
facts: Long linked to the blind pianist Maria Theresia von Paradis, though the connection is now disputed.
Leopold Mozart wept on hearing it performed during his 1785 visit to Vienna.
Its slow movement is a set of variations in G minor.

K459.about: A bright, energetic concerto notable for its march-like finale, built on a theme that returns in fugal texture near the close. It later gained an informal nickname, the ‘Second Coronation Concerto’, after Mozart performed it, alongside K. 537, at festivities in Frankfurt marking the coronation of Emperor Leopold II in 1790.
K459.ctx: Completed in December 1784 and premiered soon after, the concerto took on unexpected significance six years later, when Mozart chose it for his 1790 coronation-related concert in Frankfurt, by which time his once-brilliant Vienna career had cooled considerably.
parts: A graceful, moderate-paced intermezzo rather than a slow movement.
A vigorous finale that develops its theme fugally near the end.
facts: Nicknamed the ‘Second Coronation Concerto’ after an 1790 performance in Frankfurt.
Its finale develops its main theme in fugal counterpoint.
Has no true slow movement, using a moderate Allegretto instead.

K482.about: The first of Mozart’s piano concertos to use clarinets in place of oboes, giving it a warmer, mellower orchestral palette he would return to in his very greatest concertos. Audiences at its premiere were so moved by the slow movement that they demanded an encore, an unusual honour Mozart proudly reported to his father.
K482.ctx: Composed in December 1785, in the productive years following The Marriage of Figaro, the concerto shows Mozart increasingly folding operatic expressiveness into the concerto form, particularly in its wind-dominated slow movement.
parts: A poignant set of variations the audience demanded be repeated at its premiere.
A hunting-style rondo finale interrupted by a gentle, songful episode.
facts: The first Mozart piano concerto scored with clarinets instead of oboes.
Its slow movement was encored at the première, a rare honour.
The finale pauses for a slow, songful episode before its close.

K488.about: One of only two Mozart piano concertos to include clarinets, and among his most intimate and beloved. Its slow movement, in the rare key of F-sharp minor — the only time Mozart used that key in any work — is a solitary, siciliana-like lament unlike anything else in his concertos, framed by outer movements of unusual warmth.
K488.ctx: Composed in March 1786, alongside The Marriage of Figaro, the concerto shows Mozart at the height of his Vienna popularity turning to a more personal, confiding tone than the public brilliance of concertos like K. 482, written only months earlier.
parts: A solitary, siciliana-like lament — the only work Mozart wrote in this key.
facts: Its Adagio, in F-sharp minor, is the only piece Mozart wrote in that key.
One of only two of his piano concertos scored with clarinets.
Composed the same spring as The Marriage of Figaro.

K491.about: The darkest and most turbulent of Mozart’s piano concertos, scored for his largest orchestra, with oboes and clarinets together alongside trumpets and drums. Its stormy first movement and searching, chromatic finale left a deep impression on Beethoven, who is said to have remarked, on hearing it, that neither he nor anyone else would ever manage anything like it.
K491.ctx: Composed in the same remarkably fertile spring of 1786 as K. 488 and The Marriage of Figaro, the concerto stands apart from its immediate companion in mood, looking forward to the dramatic minor-key concertos of the Romantic era. Beethoven studied it closely, and echoes of it can be heard in his own Third Piano Concerto, also in C minor.
parts: A dark, turbulent opening movement with an unusually large orchestra.
A serene, hymn-like slow movement offering respite.
A theme-and-variations finale that ends in tragedy rather than triumph.
facts: Uses Mozart’s largest orchestra for any piano concerto, with oboes, clarinets, trumpets and drums together.
Beethoven reportedly admired it deeply and drew on it for his own C minor concerto.
Its finale, a set of variations, ends darkly rather than in triumph.

K503.about: The grandest and most symphonic of Mozart’s Vienna concertos, built on a scale approaching that of his late symphonies, with a majestic opening movement whose scope has often been compared to the ‘Jupiter’ Symphony, written two years later. Despite its scale, it remains intimate in its central slow movement, a hallmark of Mozart’s mature concerto style.
K503.ctx: Completed in December 1786, the last of Mozart’s great run of Vienna subscription-concert concertos, coming near the end of the period when he could reliably fill a concert hall as composer-performer; his popularity in Vienna would soon begin to wane.
parts: A majestic, symphonic opening movement of unusual scale.
facts: Among the largest in scale of all Mozart’s piano concertos.
Composed near the end of his most successful years as a Vienna concert pianist.
Its opening movement has been compared to the ‘Jupiter’ Symphony in scope.

K537.about: Nicknamed the ‘Coronation’ Concerto after Mozart performed it during festivities surrounding the coronation of Emperor Leopold II in Frankfurt in October 1790, alongside K. 459. Mozart left the left-hand part unwritten or only sketched across long stretches of the autograph score, implying he intended to improvise it — a reminder of how much of his concerto performances relied on spontaneous elaboration beyond what survives on the page.
K537.ctx: Composed in February 1788 but not performed publicly until Mozart’s visit to Dresden the following year and, later, at the Frankfurt coronation concert of 1790 — by which time his finances and public standing in Vienna had declined sharply from their mid-1780s peak.
facts: Its nickname comes from a 1790 performance at coronation festivities for Emperor Leopold II.
Mozart left much of the left-hand piano part unwritten in the autograph, implying improvisation.
Simpler in texture than the concertos immediately preceding it, likely for easier publication.

K595.about: Mozart’s last piano concerto and one of his final completed works, composed in the year of his death. Its autumnal, valedictory character — gentle rather than brilliant, resigned rather than triumphant — has long invited comparisons with the serenity of his very last works, though there is no firm evidence Mozart knew he was near death when he wrote it.
K595.ctx: Completed in January 1791 and premiered at one of Mozart’s last public concerts that March, the concerto shares its finale’s principal theme with the song ‘Komm, lieber Mai’, K. 596, composed the same month — a rare direct link between one of his concertos and a song.
parts: A gentle, understated opening movement, quiet rather than brilliant.
A graceful finale sharing its theme with the song ‘Komm, lieber Mai’, K. 596.
facts: Mozart’s last completed piano concerto, written in the year of his death.
Its finale shares a theme with his song ‘Komm, lieber Mai’, K. 596.
Premiered at one of Mozart’s last public concert appearances, in March 1791.

K16.about: Mozart’s first symphony, composed at age eight while the family was on its long grand tour of Europe, closely modeled on the symphonies of Johann Christian Bach, whom the young Mozart had recently met and admired in London. Simple and Italianate, in the three-movement overture form fashionable at the time.
K16.ctx: Composed during the Mozart family’s extended stay in London in 1764, where the young prodigy absorbed the galant symphonic style then dominant in the city, above all through his friendship with J. C. Bach.
parts: A slow movement whose bass line anticipates a motif Mozart would use, decades later, in the finale of his ‘Jupiter’ Symphony.
facts: Composed at age eight in London.
Closely modeled on the symphonies of J. C. Bach.
Its slow movement contains an early version of a motif Mozart reused in the ‘Jupiter’ Symphony finale twenty-four years later.

K183.about: One of only two symphonies Mozart wrote in a minor key (with No. 40, K. 550), nicknamed the ‘Little G minor’ to distinguish it from its more famous sibling. Composed at seventeen, it channels the turbulent ‘Sturm und Drang’ aesthetic fashionable in the early 1770s, with agitated, syncopated string writing throughout.
K183.ctx: Composed in October 1773, shortly after Mozart’s return from his third Italian journey, the symphony shows the influence of Haydn’s own minor-key symphonies of the period. It gained wide popular exposure two centuries later as the opening music of the 1984 film Amadeus.
parts: A calmer, more lyrical slow movement.
A stern minuet framing a gentler trio.
An agitated finale closing the symphony in its turbulent home key.
facts: One of only two Mozart symphonies in a minor key.
Used as the opening music of the 1984 film Amadeus.
Written at seventeen under the influence of Haydn’s ‘Sturm und Drang’ symphonies.

K201.about: Widely regarded as the finest of Mozart’s early symphonies, marked by refined, chamber-music-like textures and elegant contrapuntal interplay between the string sections — a considerable advance in sophistication over his earlier symphonic works.
K201.ctx: Composed in April 1774, shortly before Mozart’s eighteenth birthday, closing a highly productive period of instrumental composition in Salzburg before his attention turned increasingly to opera.
parts: An elegant opening movement built from delicate, closely worked string writing.
facts: Often ranked as the best of Mozart’s youthful symphonies.
Noted for its refined, chamber-like scoring.
Composed just before Mozart’s eighteenth birthday.

K297.about: Written for and premiered in Paris during Mozart’s unhappy job-seeking trip there in 1778, tailored to French taste with an opening orchestral unison flourish, a ‘coup d’archet’, that audiences at the Concert Spirituel reportedly loved. Mozart wrote two different versions of the slow movement after the concert’s organizer objected to the first.
K297.ctx: Composed during Mozart’s difficult 1778 stay in Paris, the same visit during which his mother, who had accompanied him, fell ill and died. Despite the personal tragedy that overshadowed the trip, the symphony was a public triumph at its premiere.
parts: A brilliant opening movement with a fashionable orchestral flourish Parisian audiences applauded.
The second of two slow movements Mozart wrote for the symphony.
facts: Mozart’s mother died in Paris during the visit that produced this symphony.
He wrote two different versions of the slow movement.
Its opening flourish was specifically calculated to please Parisian concert audiences.

K319.about: A compact, elegant symphony, composed shortly after Mozart’s return to Salzburg from the unsuccessful Paris and Mannheim job search, and originally in three movements, with a minuet added slightly later.
K319.ctx: Composed in 1779 during Mozart’s last full years in the service of the Archbishop of Salzburg, a position he found increasingly frustrating and would abandon for Vienna within two years.
parts: A minuet added to the symphony after its first version.
facts: Originally composed without a minuet, which was added afterward.
Written during Mozart’s final years in Salzburg employment.

K338.about: The last symphony Mozart composed in Salzburg before permanently relocating to Vienna, festive and brilliant in character. Like several of his other late-Salzburg symphonies it was originally written without a minuet.
K338.ctx: Composed in August 1780, shortly before Mozart travelled to Munich for the premiere of his opera Idomeneo, after which he broke decisively with his Salzburg employer, Archbishop Colloredo, and settled permanently in Vienna.
facts: The last symphony Mozart wrote while still living in Salzburg.
Composed shortly before the trip to Munich that led to his final break with the Archbishop.

K385.about: Originally composed as a serenade for the ennoblement celebrations of the Salzburg Haffner family, then reworked by Mozart into a four-movement symphony for Vienna concert use by removing a march and one of two minuets and adding flutes and clarinets to the outer movements.
K385.ctx: Written in a rush in July 1782, amid preparations for the premiere of Die Entführung aus dem Serail, at the urgent request of his father for the Haffner family celebrations. Months later, asked to rework it for a Vienna concert, Mozart reportedly wrote to his father that he was pleasantly surprised, on receiving the score back, at how good the music was — he had half forgotten it.
facts: Originally composed as a serenade, later reworked into a symphony.
Mozart reportedly forgot how good it was when the score was sent back to him months later.
Written in great haste alongside preparations for Die Entführung aus dem Serail.

K425.about: Composed in only about four days when Mozart, stopping in Linz on the way back to Vienna from Salzburg, learned a concert had been arranged in his honour and found he had no symphony on hand.
K425.ctx: Composed in late 1783 during a stop in Linz on the journey home from Salzburg, where Mozart had introduced his wife Constanze to his father for the first time. Count Johann Thun hosted the visit and arranged the impromptu concert that forced the symphony into being at such speed.
parts: A festive movement opening with Mozart’s first symphonic slow introduction.
facts: Composed in roughly four days for an unplanned concert.
The first Mozart symphony to open with a slow introduction.
Written during the trip on which Mozart first introduced his wife Constanze to his father.

K504.about: Composed for Mozart’s visit to Prague, where The Marriage of Figaro had been rapturously received. Unusually for Mozart, it has only three movements, omitting a minuet, and its expansive, contrapuntally rich opening movement anticipates the scale of his very last symphonies.
K504.ctx: Composed in December 1786 in Vienna, in anticipation of Mozart’s visit to Prague the following January, where the symphony was premiered to great acclaim during the same trip that led directly to the commission for Don Giovanni.
parts: A grand, slow-introduced opening movement of unusual contrapuntal density.
An energetic finale, with no minuet preceding it.
facts: Has no minuet, unusual among Mozart’s symphonies.
Premiered in Prague, where The Marriage of Figaro had recently been a sensation.
The visit that introduced it led directly to the commission for Don Giovanni.

K543.about: The first of Mozart’s last three symphonies, composed within about six weeks in the summer of 1788 with no known commission or occasion behind it. Festive and warm, it is notable among Mozart’s symphonies for omitting oboes entirely in favour of clarinets.
K543.ctx: Composed in June 1788, the first of an extraordinary trio of symphonies — with No. 40 and No. 41, the ‘Jupiter’ — written in rapid succession during a period of mounting financial difficulty and declining public interest in Mozart’s music, for reasons that remain unclear to scholars to this day.
parts: A stately introduction leading to a warm, expansive Allegro.
facts: First of Mozart’s last three symphonies, all written within about six weeks.
Scored with clarinets instead of the customary oboes.
No commission or occasion for the symphony is known.

K207.about: Mozart’s earliest violin concerto, composed at seventeen, modest in scale but already displaying the lyrical solo writing that would mark his mature concertos.
K207.ctx: Composed in 1773, likely for Mozart’s own use as a violinist in the Salzburg court orchestra, or for the orchestra’s leader Antonio Brunetti; its exact date has long been debated by scholars.
facts: Mozart’s first violin concerto.
Its exact date of composition was long debated before being placed in 1773.

K211.about: A concise, elegant concerto, less often performed than its four companions from the same extraordinary year, showing Mozart’s rapidly developing fluency in the genre.
K211.ctx: Composed in June 1775, the second of five violin concertos Mozart wrote in a remarkable burst within about ten months.
facts: Second of the five violin concertos Mozart wrote within about ten months in 1775.
Less frequently performed today than its companions.

K216.about: The first of Mozart’s violin concertos to enter the standard repertoire, noted for the operatic lyricism of its slow movement and a finale that unexpectedly shifts into a rustic, drone-accompanied dance episode.
K216.ctx: Composed in September 1775, part of the same extraordinary year that produced all five of Mozart’s violin concertos in quick succession.
parts: An operatic, richly lyrical slow movement.
A finale that pauses for a folk-dance-like episode in the style of a musette.
facts: Among the most frequently performed of Mozart’s five violin concertos.
Its finale includes a folk-dance episode evoking a musette.

K218.about: A brilliant, martial concerto with prominent trumpet-like fanfares in the orchestra, considered one of the more technically demanding of the five for the soloist.
K218.ctx: Composed in October 1775, the fourth of Mozart’s five violin concertos, all written within the same remarkable year.
parts: A brilliant opening movement with fanfare-like orchestral writing.
facts: Fourth of the five violin concertos Mozart composed in 1775.
Noted for its brilliant, fanfare-like orchestral writing.

K219.about: The last and most celebrated of Mozart’s violin concertos, nicknamed ‘Turkish’ for an exotic episode in the finale where the strings imitate Janissary battle music, then fashionable in Vienna.
K219.ctx: Composed in December 1775, the last of the five violin concertos Mozart wrote within a single extraordinary year — after which, though he continued playing the violin, he never returned to the concerto genre for it.
parts: A minuet-based finale interrupted by an exotic, ‘Turkish’ percussion-imitating episode.
facts: Nicknamed ‘Turkish’ for its exotic finale episode.
The last of Mozart’s five violin concertos; he never wrote another.
All five were composed within the same year, 1775.

K299.about: One of very few concertos ever written for this unusual pairing of instruments, composed on commission for a French nobleman amateur flutist and his harpist daughter.
K299.ctx: Composed in Paris in 1778 for the Duc de Guînes and his daughter, though Mozart later complained in a letter to his father that the Duke never paid him the full fee for the commission.
K299.sc: Solo flute, solo harp and orchestra
facts: Written for a French duke and his harpist daughter.
Mozart complained he was never fully paid for the commission.
One of the very few concertos written for this pairing of instruments.

K313.about: Composed on commission from a Dutch amateur flutist, part of a larger commission for flute works Mozart never fully completed — reportedly because, as he confessed in a letter to his father, he did not much like the instrument’s tone.
K313.ctx: Composed in early 1778 in Mannheim for the flutist and physician Ferdinand De Jean, whose commission for several flute works Mozart, by his own admission, struggled to find enthusiasm for.
facts: Mozart admitted in a letter that he did not particularly enjoy writing for the flute.
Commissioned by the flutist and physician Ferdinand De Jean.

K495.about: The last and most polished of Mozart’s four horn concertos, written for his old friend Joseph Leutgeb, a virtuoso horn player whom Mozart teased mercilessly in the manuscript, writing sections of the score in different coloured inks alongside joking insults aimed at the performer.
K495.ctx: Composed in 1786 for Leutgeb, a friend of the Mozart family since their Salzburg days who had since moved to Vienna and ran a cheese shop while continuing to perform; Mozart’s affectionately mocking annotations across his horn concertos are legendary among scholars.
facts: Written for Mozart’s friend Joseph Leutgeb, whom he teased affectionately in the manuscript.
The last of Mozart’s four horn concertos.

K447.about: Also written for Joseph Leutgeb, distinguished among Mozart’s horn concertos by its unusually dark orchestral scoring, using clarinets and bassoons rather than the customary oboes.
K447.ctx: Composed around 1787, part of the ongoing series of concertos and other works Mozart wrote across the 1780s for his old friend Leutgeb.
parts: An expressive opening movement in unusually rich orchestral colours.
facts: Scored with clarinets and bassoons instead of oboes, unusual for the time.
Written for Mozart’s friend Joseph Leutgeb.

K588.about: A comedy about a wager testing the constancy of two pairs of lovers, who are induced, through a cynical friend’s scheme, to test their fiancées’ fidelity by wooing each other’s partners in disguise. Its ambiguous moral tone, poised between farce and genuine emotional cost, long made it the least performed of Mozart’s mature operas, though it is now valued as highly as its companions.
K588.ctx: Composed in 1789–90 to a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte, the last of the trio of operas he wrote with Mozart, reportedly based on an idea suggested by Emperor Joseph II, though the story’s exact origins are debated by scholars.
parts: A brisk overture quoting the opera’s central ‘così fan tutte’ motto.
Fiordiligi’s defiant aria proclaiming her fidelity.
A wry, ambiguous reconciliation closing the opera.
facts: The third and last of Mozart’s operas with librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte.
Long considered morally troubling and was under-performed until the twentieth century.
Premiered less than two years before Mozart’s death.

K384.about: A rescue comedy set in a Turkish pasha’s palace, in which the hero Belmonte attempts to free his beloved Konstanze and her servants from captivity. Mozart’s first great success in Vienna, mixing spoken dialogue (Singspiel) with musical numbers, and famous for its exoticized ‘Turkish’ percussion.
K384.ctx: Composed in 1781–82 for Emperor Joseph II’s new National Singspiel company, the opera established Mozart’s reputation in Vienna. The Emperor is said to have remarked afterward that it had ‘too many notes’, to which Mozart supposedly replied that there were exactly as many as necessary — an exchange whose authenticity is disputed but that has become inseparable from the opera’s legend.
parts: A brilliant overture using exoticized ‘Turkish’ percussion.
Konstanze’s extended, technically formidable aria of defiance.
A joyful conclusion as the lovers are freed.
facts: Contains the possibly apocryphal exchange with Joseph II about ‘too many notes’.
Established Mozart’s reputation as an opera composer in Vienna.
Uses exoticized ‘Turkish’ percussion instruments to evoke its setting.

K165.about: A brilliant motet for solo soprano and orchestra, written for a celebrated castrato, ending with the famous ‘Alleluia’ that has become one of Mozart’s most frequently performed concert showpieces, independent of its original liturgical setting.
K165.ctx: Composed in Milan in January 1773 for the castrato Venanzio Rauzzini, who had just sung the lead role in Mozart’s opera Lucio Silla, as a virtuosic showcase written specifically for his voice.
facts: Written for the celebrated castrato Venanzio Rauzzini.
Its closing ‘Alleluia’ is now one of Mozart’s most popular concert excerpts.
Composed when Mozart was just seventeen.

K427.about: A large-scale, unfinished setting, among Mozart’s most ambitious sacred works, combining Baroque contrapuntal grandeur — drawn from his close study of Bach and Handel scores — with operatic vocal writing. Tradition holds it was begun as a votive offering tied to his marriage.
K427.ctx: Begun in 1782, reportedly as a vow Mozart made that he would compose a mass if Constanze recovered from illness and the couple married. It was performed incomplete at a Salzburg premiere in 1783, with Constanze herself singing one of the soprano solo parts, and Mozart never returned to finish it, leaving much of the Credo and the entire Agnus Dei unwritten.
facts: Left permanently unfinished, missing much of the Credo and the Agnus Dei entirely.
Reportedly composed as a vow connected to Mozart’s marriage to Constanze.
Constanze herself sang a soprano solo part at its 1783 premiere.

K317.about: A festive, compact mass, among Mozart’s last major sacred works written for Salzburg use. Its nickname, the ‘Coronation Mass’, was attached decades after Mozart’s death from its later use at imperial coronations, not from its original composition.
K317.ctx: Composed in 1779 for Salzburg Cathedral, part of Mozart’s official duties as court organist there during his last years in the Archbishop’s service, a position he would abandon for Vienna within two years.
parts: A tender close, its melody later echoed in the Countess’s aria ‘Dove sono’ in The Marriage of Figaro.
facts: Its ‘Coronation’ nickname comes from later use at Habsburg imperial coronations, decades after it was written.
Composed during Mozart’s final years of employment in Salzburg.
Its Agnus Dei melody resembles the Countess’s aria in The Marriage of Figaro, written seven years later.

K361.about: A monumental serenade for thirteen wind instruments, exceptionally large-scale for the genre, in seven movements including an Adagio famously used in the film Amadeus to represent the overwhelming, otherworldly beauty of Mozart’s music as heard by his rival Salieri.
K361.ctx: Composed in the early 1780s, likely for a specific Vienna wind ensemble, though the exact date and occasion remain debated among scholars; its nickname, ‘Gran Partita’, was added to the manuscript by someone other than Mozart.
parts: The first of two minuets in the work.
The famous slow movement used in the film Amadeus.
A set of variations on a simple theme.
facts: Scored for thirteen wind instruments, unusually large for a serenade.
Its Adagio was used prominently in the film Amadeus.
The nickname ‘Gran Partita’ was not written by Mozart himself.

K465.about: The last of six string quartets Mozart dedicated to Joseph Haydn, nicknamed ‘Dissonance’ for its startling, harmonically ambiguous slow introduction, full of clashing chromatic intervals left unresolved for an unusually long time before the main Allegro begins.
K465.ctx: Composed in January 1785 as the last of the ‘Haydn’ quartets, a set Mozart dedicated to the older composer in a published preface describing them as the fruit of long and laborious effort. Haydn reportedly told Mozart’s father Leopold, after hearing some of the set performed, that his son was the greatest composer he knew, either personally or by reputation.
parts: A famously dissonant slow introduction resolving into a bright Allegro.
facts: Nicknamed for its dissonant slow introduction.
The last of six quartets Mozart dedicated to Joseph Haydn.
Haydn praised Mozart to his father after hearing the set.

K516.about: One of only two string quintets Mozart wrote in a minor key, deeply tragic in tone, scored for the unusual combination of two violins, two violas and cello that gives it a darker, richer texture than a standard quartet.
K516.ctx: Composed in May 1787, the same year as Don Giovanni and shortly after the death of Mozart’s father Leopold — a connection some scholars have drawn, speculatively, to the work’s unusually somber character.
parts: A grieving introduction that turns, unexpectedly, to a consoling major-key finale.
facts: One of only two Mozart string quintets in a minor key.
Composed in the year his father died.
Uses two violas rather than two cellos, a voicing that deepens its sound.

K448.about: One of Mozart’s most brilliant chamber works, written for himself and a talented pupil to perform together, treating the two pianos as equal partners in a continuous, sparkling dialogue rather than one dominant and one accompanying.
K448.ctx: Composed in November 1781 for a concert with his pupil Josepha Auernhammer, of whom Mozart wrote unflatteringly in letters to his father even while praising her playing. Two centuries later the piece became the unlikely centrepiece of psychological research into the so-called ‘Mozart effect’.
parts: A lyrical slow movement shared equally between the two pianos.
facts: Written for Mozart and his pupil Josepha Auernhammer to perform together.
Became well known outside music circles as the piece used in 1990s research on the ‘Mozart effect’.

K304.about: One of only two Mozart violin sonatas in a minor key, composed during the difficult Paris journey during which his mother died, and often heard as carrying an unusually somber, personal weight for a genre still primarily regarded as domestic music-making.
K304.ctx: Composed in 1778, part of a set of violin sonatas written during Mozart’s unsuccessful job-seeking trip to Mannheim and Paris — a journey overshadowed by the death of his mother, who had accompanied him, in Paris that summer.
parts: A grave minuet-finale, unusual in closing a sonata rather than opening or interrupting it.
facts: One of only two Mozart violin sonatas in a minor key.
Composed around the time of his mother’s death in Paris.
Has only two movements, rather than the usual three.

K296.about: A bright, songful sonata composed for a talented young pupil in Mannheim, part of Mozart’s growing effort to give the violin a genuinely equal partnership with the piano, rather than following the older convention of a keyboard sonata with optional violin accompaniment.
K296.ctx: Composed in March 1778 for Thérèse Pierron Serrarius, a young pupil in Mannheim whose family hosted Mozart during part of his stay there.
facts: Written for a young pupil in Mannheim, Thérèse Pierron Serrarius.
Part of Mozart’s development of the violin sonata toward true instrumental partnership.

K397.about: An improvisatory, dramatic fantasia, left unfinished by Mozart and completed by a later hand with a short closing Allegretto. Its brooding opening and free, rhapsodic structure make it one of Mozart’s most Romantic-sounding keyboard works.
K397.ctx: Composed around 1782 but not published until after Mozart’s death, when it appeared with an ending supplied by someone other than Mozart to bring the fragment to a satisfying close.
facts: Left unfinished at the point Mozart stopped composing it; its familiar ending was supplied by a later hand.
Among the most improvisatory and Romantic in feeling of Mozart’s keyboard works.

K475.about: A large-scale, dramatic fantasia Mozart published together with his C minor Piano Sonata, K. 457, as a paired introduction to the sonata. Harmonically wide-ranging and structurally free, it alternates stormy and lyrical episodes across a single continuous span.
K475.ctx: Composed in 1785, shortly before the sonata K. 457 with which it was published as a pair the following year; both works are dedicated, like several of Mozart’s Vienna-period pieces, to his pupil Therese von Trattner.
facts: Published together with the Piano Sonata in C minor, K. 457, as a paired introduction.
Dedicated, like the sonata, to Mozart’s pupil Therese von Trattner.

K485.about: A graceful, good-humoured rondo, lighter in tone than Mozart’s darker fantasias and rondos of the period, built on a charming, dance-like main theme.
K485.ctx: Composed in January 1786, around the time Mozart was completing The Marriage of Figaro, offering a lighter contrast within his keyboard output that year.
facts: Composed the same year as The Marriage of Figaro.
Lighter and more good-humoured than Mozart’s other keyboard rondos of the period.

K511.about: One of Mozart’s most deeply expressive solo keyboard works, an extended, melancholy rondo whose wandering chromatic harmony anticipates the emotional world of later Romantic piano music.
K511.ctx: Composed in March 1787, the same year as the String Quintet K. 516 and shortly before his father’s death — a period that produced several of Mozart’s most inward, minor-key works.
facts: Widely regarded as one of Mozart’s most emotionally profound short piano pieces.
Composed in 1787, a year that produced several of his darkest, most inward works.

K265.about: A set of light, virtuosic variations on the French folk tune familiar in English as ‘Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star’, written partly as an accessible teaching piece and partly as a display of Mozart’s inventive variation technique.
K265.ctx: Composed around 1781–82, probably for use with Mozart’s own pupils, on a tune already widely known and used by other composers of the period as a theme for variations.
facts: Based on the tune known in English as ‘Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star’.
One of Mozart’s most widely recognized melodies today, though its fame rests on the borrowed folk tune rather than an original theme.

K540.about: One of Mozart’s darkest and most harmonically searching solo keyboard works, standing entirely alone rather than paired with another movement, its grief-laden chromaticism unusual even among his minor-key pieces.
K540.ctx: Composed in March 1788, the same eventful year that produced his last three symphonies, during a period of increasing financial difficulty and declining public fortune in Vienna.
facts: Stands as a complete, independent single movement rather than part of a larger work.
Composed in 1788, the same year as Mozart’s last three symphonies.

K574.about: A brief, spirited keyboard gigue written into the autograph album of the Leipzig court organist, whimsically chromatic and contrapuntally playful, evoking the Baroque dance-suite tradition of J. S. Bach, whose manuscripts Mozart had recently studied.
K574.ctx: Composed in May 1789 during Mozart’s visit to Leipzig, where he examined manuscripts of J. S. Bach at the Thomaskirche — an experience that left a visible mark on this brief, contrapuntally dense miniature.
facts: Written during Mozart’s visit to Leipzig, where he studied J. S. Bach’s manuscripts.
Shows unusually dense, Bach-influenced counterpoint for such a short piece.
